ch6_ex5_q1: Sense check: the answer must be less than the big semicircle alone ($12.5\pi \approx 39.3$), because more is cut out than added.
ch6_ex5_q2: Net effect: two semicircles out and one in means just one semicircle out: $90 - \frac{1}{2}\pi \times 2.5^2 = 90 - 3.125\pi \approx 80.18$.
Elimination: the answer must be a bit less than 90 (D is the plain rectangle), which leaves only C.
ch6_ex5_q3: Difference of squares: $7^2 - 2^2 = 9 \times 5 = 45$, and $\frac{330}{360} = \frac{11}{12}$, so the area is $\frac{11}{12} \times 45\pi = 41.25\pi$.
ch6_ex5_q4: Factorise: $2\pi r^2 + \pi r l = \pi r(2r + l) = 28\pi(56 + 40) = 2688\pi \approx 8444.6$.
Since both parts share $r = 28$, keeping $\pi$ as a common factor means only one calculator step.
ch6_ex5_q5b: The average of the parallel sides is $12.5$, and $12.5 \times 8 = 100$. Multiplying by 8 is the same as doubling three times.
ch6_ex5_q5c: Check another way: since $7^2 = 3^2 + 5^2 + 3 \times 5$, the angle opposite the 7 is $120^\circ$. Then $\frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 5 \times \sin 120^\circ \approx 6.50$, matching Heron.
ch6_ex5_q6a: Exact: $\pi \times 6 \times 3 = 18\pi$. That is exactly half of a circle of radius 6, because the ellipse is squashed to half height.
ch6_ex5_q6b: Half of the $10 \times 12$ rectangle drawn around the rhombus: $\frac{120}{2} = 60$.
ch6_ex5_q7a: Slide the semicircle cut from the left end across to fill the right end: you are left with a plain $20 \times 15$ rectangle, so no $\pi$ is needed.
ch6_ex5_q7c: Alternative split: a $20 \times 5$ rectangle on the bottom ($100$) plus a trapezium on top with parallel sides 10 and 14 and height 5 ($60$) gives 160.
The bounding box ($20 \times 10 = 200$) is a quick upper limit to check against.
ch6_ex5_q8a: Exact form: $225\pi - 207$. This makes it easy to see the circle is about 707 and the triangle takes away 207.
ch6_ex5_q8b: A quarter-circle segment is always $\left(\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\right)r^2 \approx 0.285r^2$. Here $0.285 \times 156.25 \approx 44.6$.
ch6_ex5_q8c: Each circle sits in its own $10 \times 10$ square and leaves $1 - \frac{\pi}{4} \approx 21.5\%$ uncovered, so the shaded area is $21.5\%$ of 600, about 129.
ch6_ex5_q9b: Exact: $\pi \times 14 \times (14 + 20) = 476\pi$. The curved part ($280\pi$) is bigger than the base ($196\pi$) because $l > r$.
ch6_ex5_q10a: Exact height: $\sqrt{14^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{160} = 4\sqrt{10} \approx 12.65$, so each end is $24\sqrt{10}$.
The three rectangles together are perimeter $\times$ length: $40 \times 18 = 720$, which is most of the answer.
ch6_ex5_q10b: Shortcut: full TSA of the big cylinder plus only the curved side of the small one: $238\pi + 40\pi = 278\pi \approx 873.36$.
ch6_ex5_q10c: Spot the 5-12-13 Pythagorean triple: half the base is 5 and the height is 12, so the slant height is exactly 13.
ch6_ex5_q11a: Worth memorising the cubes up to $10^3$: $7^3 = 343$ comes up often.
ch6_ex5_q11c: Exact: $\pi \times 1225 \times 40 = 49\,000\pi$. Estimate: $3 \times 49\,000 = 147\,000$, a bit under the answer.
ch6_ex5_q12a: Exact: $\frac{1}{2}\pi \times 0.5^2 \times 3.7 = 0.4625\pi$. Remember the radius is $0.5$ m, not 1 m.
ch6_ex5_q13a: Cancel the third into the base area: $\frac{81}{3} = 27$, then $27 \times 11 = 297$.
ch6_ex5_q14a: Path shortcut: perimeter $\times$ width $+ 4 \times$ width$^2$ $= 58 \times 1 + 4 = 62\text{ m}^2$.
ch6_ex5_q15: Test it: $r = 1, h = 6$ gives $6\pi$; $r = 3, h = 1$ gives $9\pi$, which is 1.5 times bigger.
ch6_ex5_q16: Factor $= \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 2 = 3$. The order of the changes doesn't matter because multiplication can be done in any order.
ch6_ex5_q17b: 5 cents per $\text{cm}^2$ is the same as dividing the area by 20: $3606.55 \div 20 \approx \$180.33$.
ch6_ex5_q17c: Write it as $\pi r^2\left(h + \frac{2}{3}r\right) = 196\pi\left(20 + \frac{28}{3}\right)$. The hemisphere acts like an extra $\frac{2}{3}r$ of cylinder.
ch6_ex5_q17d: Exact: old holder $= \frac{1}{4}\pi \times 324 \times 35 = 2835\pi$, so the difference is $\frac{17\,248\pi}{3} - 2835\pi = \frac{8743\pi}{3}$.
ch6_ex5_q18a: Sense check: the slant height (1.33 m) must be longer than both the cone height (1.1 m) and the radius (0.75 m).
ch6_ex5_q18b: Work out one silo fully (about $28.47\text{ m}^2$) before multiplying by 32, and keep the unrounded value so the final answer is accurate.
ch6_ex5_q18c: Painted area $= 32 \times (\text{one silo} - \text{its base}) \approx 854.4\text{ m}^2$; $854.4 \div 40 \approx 21.4$ L, so 22 whole litres if paint only comes in litres.
ch6_ex5_q18d: The cone top holds the same as a cylinder of height $\frac{1.1}{3}$, so each silo acts like a cylinder of height $5 + \frac{1.1}{3} \approx 5.37$ m: $\pi \times 0.75^2 \times 5.37 \approx 9.48\text{ m}^3$.
ch6_ex5_q18e: Each truck holds $2.4 \times 5 \times 2.5 = 30\text{ m}^3$; $303.48 \div 30 \approx 10.1$, so the 11th truck carries only about $3.5\text{ m}^3$.
ch6_ex5_q18f: Rates: $\frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{m}^3/\text{min}} = \text{min}$. At this rate, emptying all the silos takes $303.48 \div 2.5 \approx 121$ minutes, about 2 hours.
ch6_ex5_q19a: The parallel sun rays plus the line through C and A form a 'Z' shape, so the angle at the stick equals the angle at the Earth's centre.
ch6_ex5_q19b: This is a sector question in disguise: the arc is the same fraction of the circumference as the angle is of $360^\circ$.
ch6_ex5_q19c: Error $= 6380 - 6263 = 117$ km, and $\frac{117}{6380} \approx 0.018$, so less than 2%. Remarkably accurate for a stick and a shadow.
